title: What Changed
briefing.company: Antojo is a food-ordering app: people order from neighborhood restaurants, the restaurants cook, couriers deliver. Orders go through web-gateway to orders-api, which asks inventory-api whether each dish is available and writes the order to orders-db. Each service belongs to a different team.
briefing.role: You're on call for orders this week. It's Friday night, technically Saturday. The late-night taquerías are still taking orders.
runbook.ordersErrors.title: orders-api is failing orders
runbook.ordersErrors.body:
orders-api takes an order from the app, checks every dish with inventory-api and writes the order to orders-db. A 500 from orders-api means one of those steps failed, or orders-api failed on its own.

Start with what changed in the last hours: deploys, flags and database settings, for every service, not just orders-api. orders-api's own deploys are the easy suspect; they are not the only one.

Then find the step that fails: orders-api's error logs name it, and its client metrics show whether the calls to inventory-api and orders-db succeed.

Restarting orders-api drops in-flight orders and undoes nothing that changed. Use it only if you know why.
runbook.inventory.title: inventory-api (dish availability)
runbook.inventory.body:
inventory-api answers, for each dish in an order, whether the restaurant can make it right now. It reads from inventory-cache and belongs to the inventory team, who deploy on their own schedule.

orders-api 7.10 and later read two fields from every availability answer: available and prep_minutes. prep_minutes was added in inventory-api 4.2.0; older versions do not send it.

Releases run unit tests and a smoke test of inventory-api itself. Nothing checks a release against the fields orders-api reads.

Moving inventory-api to another version, back or forward, takes about six minutes, one instance at a time.
runbook.ordersDb.title: orders-db (shared database)
runbook.ordersDb.body:
orders-db holds every order. orders-api writes to it; the nightly export reads from it. Parameter changes belong to the DBA on call and reload without a restart.

The nightly export (export-job) starts at 02:40 and copies the day's orders to the data warehouse in 60 batches, until around 06:00. Each batch locks the orders table in SHARE mode for one to three seconds so the copy is consistent. Writes that arrive during a batch wait for the lock; lock_timeout decides how long they may wait before the database cancels them.

The data team is moving orders to a new schema, orders_v2, in four steps. Each step sits behind a feature flag the data team owns.

mitigation.restart-orders.what: Fresh processes, same code and settings. Drops in-flight orders for about a minute.

prompt.renata.ask: Restaurants are calling: customers say the app won't take their orders. How many orders are failing, and what do I tell the restaurants?
distractor.ordersDeploy: Tonight's orders-api deploy broke order placement.
distractor.exportCpu: The nightly export ran orders-db out of CPU.
distractor.cacheRefresh: The menu cache refresh left inventory-api answering with stale data.
chain.customers: About one order in eight fails; restaurants never see it
variant.a.change.inventory: inventory-api 4.3.0: availability grouped under stock for the new menu screens
variant.a.change.orders: orders-api 7.12.0: copy changes on the order confirmation
variant.a.change.config: vacuum the orders table more often
variant.a.factor.shape: An inventory-api release moved the available field under stock, and orders-api cannot read the new answer.
variant.a.factor.strictDecode: orders-api fails the whole order when it cannot read a field from inventory-api, even though the call itself succeeds.
variant.a.factor.noContractTest: inventory-api releases are tested only against inventory-api itself: nothing checks the fields orders-api reads.
variant.a.chain.noContract: inventory-api releases skip any check against what orders-api reads
variant.a.chain.strict: orders-api fails the order when a field is missing
variant.a.chain.decode: inventory-api answers 200, orders-api cannot read it
variant.a.debriefNote: orders-api paged, and orders-api had deployed minutes later, but the errors began with inventory-api's release. Every call to inventory-api succeeded; orders-api just could not read what came back. A release that changes a response changes every service that reads it, and nothing in inventory-api's pipeline knew what orders-api reads.
variant.b.change.inventory: inventory-api 4.2.3: faster cache warm-up after restarts
variant.b.change.orders: orders-api 7.12.1: round tips to the cent on the receipt
variant.b.change.flag: orders_v2 migration step 2 of 4: start dual-writing orders
variant.b.change.config: more sort memory for the weekly reports
variant.b.factor.dualWrite: The data team turned on dual-write to the new orders_v2 table, and orders-api now writes every order twice.
variant.b.factor.constraint: orders_v2 requires a kitchen_tz value that orders-api does not send, so the database rejects the second write and the order fails with it.
variant.b.factor.unannounced: A flag owned by another team changes orders-api's write path, and nobody on orders-api hears when it flips: no ticket, no announcement.
variant.b.chain.unannounced: Another team's flag changes orders-api's writes without a ticket
variant.b.chain.constraint: orders_v2 requires kitchen_tz, which orders-api does not send
variant.b.chain.rejected: orders-db rejects the second write and the order fails
variant.b.debriefNote: orders-api's own deploy landed after the errors began, and orders-api's code had not changed in a way that mattered. A flag owned by the data team changed what orders-api does with every order, and the new table refused rows the old one accepted. Switching the flag back was the fix, and nobody on orders-api had been told it would flip tonight.
variant.c.change.orders: orders-api 7.12.2: new receipt footer for partner restaurants
variant.c.change.config: fail fast instead of piling up behind locks (action item from last month's incident)
variant.c.factor.lockTimeout: A database change at 23:10 lowered lock_timeout on orders-db from 5 s to 200 ms.
variant.c.factor.exportLocks: From 02:40 the nightly export locks the orders table for one to three seconds per batch.
variant.c.factor.staging: Database parameter changes are tested on staging, where the nightly export never runs.
variant.c.chain.staging: Parameter changes are tested on staging, which has no nightly jobs
variant.c.chain.export: 02:40 · the nightly export locks the orders table for seconds at a time
variant.c.chain.giveUp: Order inserts give up after 200 ms instead of waiting out the batch
variant.c.debriefNote: The errors started at 02:40, the moment the export did, and three and a half hours after the change that caused them. The latest change, orders-api's deploy, was innocent. The 23:10 setting was harmless all evening because nothing held locks; the export was harmless every other night because writes could wait. Neither was the cause alone, and matching the onset time only found half of it.
variant.d.change.inventory: rollback inventory-api to 4.1.3: stock counts lagging since 4.2.0 (INV-208)
variant.d.change.orders: orders-api 7.12.3: clearer error when a restaurant closes mid-order
variant.d.change.flag: suggested tips on checkout for the weekend
variant.d.change.config: log more slow statements for the index review
variant.d.factor.rollback: inventory-api was rolled back from 4.2.2 to 4.1.3, which does not send prep_minutes.
variant.d.factor.prepMinutes: orders-api 7.10 and later need prep_minutes in every availability answer, a field inventory-api only sends since 4.2.0.
variant.d.factor.unchecked: Rollbacks skip the deploy pipeline's checks, so nothing asked whether the older release still gave other services what they need.
variant.d.chain.needs: orders-api needs prep_minutes, sent only since inventory-api 4.2.0
variant.d.chain.decode: inventory-api answers 200, orders-api cannot read it
variant.d.debriefNote: A rollback feels like the opposite of a change, but it is one: it took away a field that orders-api had needed since inventory-api 4.2.0. The inventory team was fixing a real problem of their own, and the rollback skipped the checks a release would have had. The way out was forward, to the version that came before tonight.
